doc_summary: Marks argues practical interpretability should target problems that standard ML (data plus behavioral oversight) structurally cannot solve, such as secret elicitation, alignment fakers, sandbagging, and honeypot realism. The post treats the difficulty of building realistic inputs that fool a model into believing an opportunity is real as a core motivating obstruction.

items.claim: Identifies that synthetic inputs designed to convince a model it has a real opportunity often carry tells that reveal they are tests, so behavioral data cannot separate a genuinely aligned model from a lying-in-wait faker.
items.quote: You try to make synthetic inputs that fool the model into believing it has such an opportunity, but there might be tells that the opportunity isn't real (e.g. maybe the model is waiting to see near-impossible-to-fake evidence that it's been deployed

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence of good behavior on test inputs, because an aligned model and an evaluation-aware faker behave identically on every input the auditor can think to test.
items.quote: on all the episodes you have access to, an aligned model and an alignment-faker-in-wait will, by assumption, behave identically.

items.claim: Treats whether a model is thinking about being in an evaluation, in a causally relevant way for its outputs, as the key property to check, shown by whether changing its belief about being evaluated changes its behavior.
items.quote: The one on the right is thinking about whether it's in an evaluation, whereas the one on the left is not. Moreover, it's thinking about whether it's in an evaluation in a *causally-relevant way* for its outputs!

items.claim: In a setup, do not rely only on making a scenario look realistic, because realistic opportunity and honeypot-ness can be coupled; instead intervene on the model's belief that the input is a honeypot to trigger the behavior.
items.quote: it might be that any input we make which appears to present a realistic opportunity to strike, also looks like a clear honeypot. In this case, we might attempt using interpretability techniques to modify the model's beliefs about whether an input is a honeypot

items.claim: Names the two conditions a trigger needs, a genuine opportunity and not being a honeypot, and notes that auditors can often produce each separately but not jointly.
items.quote: we have access to inputs on which *A* is true and inputs on which *B* is true, but no inputs on which *A* and *B* are both true (e.g. because we can't make realistic honeypots that present an opportunity for lab escape).

items.claim: Prefers problems that cannot be detected behaviorally over easily elicited behaviors, because standard ML baselines will beat interpretability on the latter.
items.quote: If you're trying to solve a problem involving a model behavior that's easy to elicit and detect, it's unlikely interpretability-based techniques will beat the best traditional ML baselines

items.claim: Prefers evidence that holds up against a strong, simple baseline (such as prompting the model) over positive results that a baseline would also have achieved, because otherwise the added technique is unproven.
items.quote: in all the cases I know of, "ask the model to label the statement with a well-tuned prompt" would have been a very strong baseline. Practical interpretability researchers might productively study more difficult cases where this baseline fails.

items.claim: Warns that elicited confessions or secrets may be false when there is no independent way to verify them, so apparent revelations are not automatically convincing evidence.
items.quote: Since you might not have an independent way to verify what the model tells you, you need to worry about "false confessions"—verbalizations of apparent secrets which the model does not actually believe.

items.claim: Prefers model-organism testbeds where the ground truth is known by construction, such as a trained secret or backdoor, while noting that a setup is weak if the answer can be guessed from the model's own hints.
items.quote: Note, though, that this isn't an ideal setting, since you might be able to guess the word just by figuring it out from the model's hints.

items.claim: Is skeptical of published claims about reasoning models that behave differently when they believe they are being evaluated.
items.quote: Though note that I'm skeptical about many of the claims made in this paper.
